alert2.typicalNote: the mean of the real recordings

betweenBursts.unit: cores one channel takes while nothing is on the air (0.05 is 5 % of one core)

windowNotes.1200000: measured because it is one of the three windows a Raspberry Pi 4 figure exists for
windowNotes.1440000: the window Flood-Net's four channels need

agentOwnMeasure.note: the agent's own measurement (lib/devices/sdr-bench.js), as its settings page shows it, rounded to 0.001 of a core

asAgentMeasures.note: the same loop as the agent's own measurement, unrounded: what the Raspberry Pi 4 figures are compared with

asDecoderThreadFirstChannel.note: with the settings the decoder threads really run with since agent 0.19, spectrum on: a stick's first channel

asDecoderThreadOtherChannels.note: the same with the spectrum off: a stick's other channels

parallel.note: the between-bursts loop at 1.44 MHz (set up as a decoder thread is) in 4 threads started together and run for the same 1000 ms, against one alone; 3 runs together and 4 alone, the least of each. 1.0 means a channel costs the same with every core busy. A ratio under 1 can only be something else disturbing the runs alone, so the slowdown is never put under 1.

memory.note: memory each of 4 real decoder threads adds on a 1.44 MHz window after six seconds of samples (the middle of three runs), with nothing queued. A decoder that falls behind may queue up to 20 s of samples on top (lib/devices/sdr.js, lines 70-81).

traffic.note: One channel in a 240 kHz window through the agent's real decoder thread (lib/devices/sdr-worker.js): 32 s of made-up signal a scenario, 20-25 dB over the noise, fed as fast as the thread takes it after an untimed warm-up of ten seconds of the same kind of traffic. measuredCores = the time it took / the seconds of signal. The stream starts and ends with a quiet stretch, so it holds a little under the rate named: msABurst is what each burst added over a quiet channel, and cores = the quiet channel + the bursts a minute named x msABurst — the share of one core at that rate. 1 or more means the thread could not keep up with a real radio.

scenarios.what: legacy ALERT, 8 bursts a minute (a busy day)
legacy ALERT, 20 bursts a minute (a storm)
ALERT2, 20 frames a minute of 74 bytes (about what one ALERT2 link carries today)
ALERT2 with every half-second slot used: 120 frames a minute of 54 bytes (the most the protocol allows)
ALERT2, a 350-byte frame every 2.5 s: 24 a minute, on the air three quarters of the time

timesARaspberryPi4.standing: Nobody has run this tool on a Raspberry Pi 4 yet. The comparison rests on three figures taken on a busy Pi 4 with an older agent, and one round figure from a sentence. Treat it as a rough guide.
timesARaspberryPi4.how: perCore: the geometric mean of (a Pi 4's cores a channel) / (this computer's cores a channel) between bursts, at the windows a Pi 4 figure exists for. wholeComputer: perCore x the cores this computer really has with all of them busy (4 / 1.12) / a Pi 4's 4 cores.
timesARaspberryPi4.likeForLikeNote: The Pi 4 figures were taken with agent 0.15 and this is agent 0.23.1: not strictly like for like.

betweenBursts.reference: the share of one core a channel takes between bursts, by the agent's own built-in measurement, on the Raspberry Pi 4 of the first base station
betweenBursts.source: RPi ALERT docs/roadmap.md, lines 112-113: "the bench says 240 kHz 6%, 1.2 MHz 27%, 1.44 MHz 31% a channel"

960000.note: no Raspberry Pi 4 figure: docs/hardware.md, lines 66-73, gives only "3x a 240 kHz channel"

2400000.note: no Raspberry Pi 4 figure: docs/hardware.md, lines 66-73, gives only "6.3x a 240 kHz channel"

caveats: Taken in October 2026 with agent 0.15, older than the agent measured here. Agent 0.17 says it cut the work between bursts by about a quarter (docs/roadmap.md, lines 78-80); the same Pi 4 has not been measured since.

The agent takes this measurement by itself a minute and a half after it starts (lib/agent.js, lines 50-52), while its channels are already decoding. That Pi 4 was a working base station with eight channels and its screen dashboard on (docs/hardware.md, lines 101-106). A measurement that has to share the processor reads high, which makes a Pi 4 look slower than it is and any other computer look faster against it.

burstFull.reference: one burst's decode with the Full decoder: about 1000 ms
burstFull.source: RPi ALERT docs/hardware.md, lines 76-77: "A burst's decode — a second or so on a Pi 4"
burstFull.caveat: A round figure in a sentence, for no named recording: a rough ratio only.

burstLean.reference: the Lean decoder took 33-34 % of the Full decoder's time on that Pi 4, over 11,628 live bursts
burstLean.caveat: A share of the Full decoder's time, not milliseconds: there is no Raspberry Pi 4 figure in milliseconds for Lean.

burstLight.source: RPi ALERT docs/configuration.md, lines 130-134 (figures from a PC)
burstLight.caveat: No Raspberry Pi 4 figure for the Light decoder.

alert2.source: RPi ALERT docs/configuration.md, lines 119-120: "a few tenths of a second on a Pi 4"
alert2.caveat: Words only: no figure to divide by.

underLoad.source: RPi ALERT docs/roadmap.md, lines 113-114: "under load each decoder's busy share ran about 1.6 times that"
underLoad.caveat: Seen on that one Pi 4 only. Used here as a safety margin on every computer.

capacity.how: For each channel: 1.6 x its between-bursts cores (the margin a loaded Raspberry Pi 4 needed) + its burst work at the traffic named. "comfortably" keeps the total under 50 % of the cores this computer has with all of them busy, and each channel under 70 % of one core. "atTheVeryMost" uses all of it: do not plan to it. Memory: half of it, less the agent, over a channel's memory and the most it may queue.
capacity.betweenBursts: filtering every sample (the setting the agent ships with)

busy.what: legacy ALERT, 8 bursts a minute on every channel (a busy day)

storm.what: legacy ALERT, 20 bursts a minute on every channel (a storm)

alert2Today.what: ALERT2 on every channel at 20 frames a minute (what one ALERT2 link carries today)

channelsToday.traffic: a storm on every channel: 20 bursts a minute, legacy ALERT or ALERT2, whichever costs more

capacity.notMeasured: The radio sticks, USB, the rtl_sdr program, the agent's own main thread and the screen dashboard are not in these figures.

alert2Headroom.rule: at least 4 cores, each at least 2.5 times a Raspberry Pi 4 core
alert2Headroom.why: Each channel is decoded on one core and can never use more than one. An ALERT2 channel with every half-second slot used is more work than one Raspberry Pi 4 core can do, however many cores there are.

directCheck.what: one channel in a 1.44 MHz window with every half-second ALERT2 slot used
directCheck.formula: 1.6 x between-bursts cores at 1.44 MHz + (alert2-every-slot - quiet)

checks.check: four channels on one stick in a 1.44 MHz window (Flood-Net's four), a storm of legacy ALERT on every one
checks.formula: 4 x (1.6 x between-bursts cores at 1.44 MHz + (legacy-heavy - quiet))

checks.check: eight channels on two sticks in 960 kHz windows, ALERT2 on every one at today's rate
checks.formula: 8 x (1.6 x between-bursts cores at 960 kHz + (alert2-today - quiet))

checks.check: one ALERT2 channel with every half-second slot used, in a 1.44 MHz window
checks.formula: 1.6 x between-bursts cores at 1.44 MHz + (alert2-every-slot - quiet)

selfCheck.note: Every recording and every made-up burst has a known right answer. A computer that reads one wrongly should not be used until that is understood.

text: open-ALERT base station benchmark 1.0.0 — full run, took 3 min 58 s
Computer   Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz
4 cores, 15.7 GB memory, x86-64 (Intel or AMD), a virtual machine
System     Ubuntu 24.04.5 LTS, Node v22.23.4
Agent      RPi ALERT 0.23.1 in .../RPi_ALERT/agent
Label      Shared 4-core virtual machine (cloud sandbox), Linux 6.18
NOTE: This computer was already busy when the run began (load 1.39), so the figures will come out
worse than it really is. Run it again when the computer is idle.
IN SHORT
One core of this computer     about 4.8 times a Raspberry Pi 4 core (3.6 to 5.3, depending on the measure)
The whole computer            about 4.3 Raspberry Pi 4s
Channels it carries today     12 comfortably, 24 at the very most (in a 1.44 MHz window, a storm on every channel)
ALERT2 headroom rule          PASSES — 4 cores (4 needed), each about 4.8 times a Pi 4 core (2.5 needed)
Decoder check                 every recording and test burst was read correctly on this computer
The two Raspberry Pi 4 lines rest on very few Pi 4 figures, taken on a busy Pi 4: read "How far to
trust the Raspberry Pi 4 comparison" below. The channel count does not use them.
This measures decoding only. The radio sticks, USB and the screen dashboard are not in it, and
nothing here has been run with a real radio stick on a computer that is not a Raspberry Pi.
WHAT WAS MEASURED ON THIS COMPUTER
All with the agent's own decoder code. A "core" is one of the processor's cores: each channel is
decoded on one of them. "Legacy ALERT" is the older protocol most stations still send; ALERT2 is
its successor.
Decoding one burst — milliseconds of one core, on real recordings off the air
Full    Lean   Light
a strong burst, recorded off the air                     259      96      45
a weak burst, recorded off the air                       301      90      47
a test-rig burst (a three-second recording)              270     107      51
Lean is the decoder the agent uses unless it is told otherwise.
An ALERT2 burst — milliseconds of one core (Lean decoder)
a real frame of 74 bytes, recorded off the air           164   (91 tried as a legacy burst first, then 73 as ALERT2)
a real frame of 33 bytes, recorded off the air           124   (76 tried as a legacy burst first, then 47 as ALERT2)
a made-up frame of 54 bytes (0.32 s on the air)          125   (80 tried as a legacy burst first, then 45 as ALERT2)
a made-up frame of 150 bytes (0.8 s on the air)          197   (129 tried as a legacy burst first, then 69 as ALERT2)
a made-up frame of 350 bytes (1.84 s on the air)         313   (195 tried as a legacy burst first, then 118 as ALERT2)
a made-up frame of 500 bytes (2.55 s on the air)         402   (260 tried as a legacy burst first, then 143 as ALERT2)
A typical ALERT2 burst costs 1.6 times a legacy burst, because it is tried as one first.
A channel while nothing is on the air — share of one core
The "window" is the slice of the band a radio stick listens to at once; a wider one holds
channels further apart and costs more.
240 kHz window                                         0.8 %
960 kHz window                                         4.0 %
1.2 MHz window                                         4.7 %
1.44 MHz window                                        5.6 %   (the window Flood-Net's four channels need)
2.4 MHz window                                         9.1 %
With all 4 cores busy at once, a channel costs 1.12 times as much as on its own.
Memory — 49 MB for each channel, on top of 52 MB for the agent itself.
One channel under traffic, through the agent's real decoder thread — share of one core (Lean decoder, 240 kHz window)
nothing on the air                                     1.2 %
legacy ALERT, 8 bursts a minute                        2.2 %   4 of 4 read
legacy ALERT, 20 bursts a minute                       3.7 %   10 of 10 read
ALERT2, 20 frames a minute                             6.9 %   10 of 10 read
ALERT2, every half-second slot used                   36.8 %   57 of 57 read
ALERT2, long frames, 24 a minute                      16.2 %   12 of 12 read
8 legacy bursts a minute is a busy day and 20 a storm. 20 ALERT2 frames a minute is about what
one ALERT2 link carries today; every half-second slot used (120 a minute) is the most the
protocol allows.
HOW MANY CHANNELS
Worked out from this computer's own figures above, not from the Raspberry Pi 4 comparison. Each
channel is counted as 1.6 times its share while nothing is on the air (the margin a loaded
Raspberry Pi 4 needed) plus its traffic. "Comfortably" keeps half the computer free for a storm,
the radio sticks' own work, the web page and a screen dashboard. "At the very most" leaves
nothing: do not plan to it.
Channels: comfortably / at the very most            busy day           storm    ALERT2 today
in a 960 kHz window                                  23 / 47         19 / 39         14 / 29
in a 2.4 MHz window                                  11 / 22         10 / 20          8 / 17
busy day: legacy ALERT, 8 bursts a minute on every channel. storm: 20 a minute. ALERT2 today:
every channel an ALERT2 link at 20 frames a minute.
Memory is enough for 76 channels in a 1.44 MHz window.
A radio stick carries at most 8 channels, and only channels close enough together to fit its
window, so 12 channels need at least 2 sticks.
Three set layouts, checked the same way:
fits      four channels on one stick in a 1.44 MHz window (Flood-Net's four), a storm of legacy
ALERT on every one: 13 % of this computer (the limit is 50 %)
fits      eight channels on two sticks in 960 kHz windows, ALERT2 on every one at today's rate:
27 % of this computer (the limit is 50 %)
fits      one ALERT2 channel with every half-second slot used, in a 1.44 MHz window: 45 % of one
core (the limit is 70 %)
THE ALERT2 HEADROOM RULE: PASSES
The rule: at least 4 cores, each at least 2.5 times a Raspberry Pi 4 core.
Why: Each channel is decoded on one core and can never use more than one. An ALERT2 channel with
every half-second slot used is more work than one Raspberry Pi 4 core can do, however many cores
there are.
This computer: 4 cores; one core is about 4.8 times a Raspberry Pi 4 core (between 3.6 and 5.3,
measure by measure).
The same question asked of this computer's own figures, without the Raspberry Pi 4 ones: one
channel in a 1.44 MHz window with every half-second ALERT2 slot used would take 45 % of the one
core it runs on (the limit is 70 %): it fits.
HOW FAR TO TRUST THE RASPBERRY PI 4 COMPARISON
Nobody has run this tool on a Raspberry Pi 4 yet. The comparison rests on three figures taken on a
busy Pi 4 with an older agent, and one round figure from a sentence. Treat it as a rough guide.
- RPi ALERT docs/roadmap.md, lines 112-113: "the bench says 240 kHz 6%, 1.2 MHz 27%, 1.44 MHz 31%
a channel". These are the share of one core a channel takes between bursts, by the agent's own
built-in measurement, on the Raspberry Pi 4 of the first base station. Taken in October 2026
with agent 0.15, older than the agent measured here. Agent 0.17 says it cut the work between
bursts by about a quarter (docs/roadmap.md, lines 78-80); the same Pi 4 has not been measured
since. The agent takes this measurement by itself a minute and a half after it starts
(lib/agent.js, lines 50-52), while its channels are already decoding. That Pi 4 was a working
base station with eight channels and its screen dashboard on (docs/hardware.md, lines 101-106).
A measurement that has to share the processor reads high, which makes a Pi 4 look slower than it
is and any other computer look faster against it.
- RPi ALERT docs/hardware.md, lines 76-77: "A burst's decode — a second or so on a Pi 4". A round
figure in a sentence, for no named recording: a rough ratio only.
- RPi ALERT docs/roadmap.md, lines 113-114: "under load each decoder's busy share ran about 1.6
times that". Seen on that one Pi 4 only. Used here as a safety margin on every computer.
There is no Raspberry Pi 4 figure at all for a 960 kHz or 2.4 MHz window, for the Lean or Light
decoders in milliseconds, or for ALERT2. (Line numbers are those of RPi ALERT commit 37fee8b (10
November 2026).)
Measure by measure, a core of this computer came out at: 240 kHz 4.1, 1.2 MHz 5.2, 1.44 MHz 5.3;
and by the round "a second or so" for a Full decode, about 3.6 times a Raspberry Pi 4 core. The Pi
4 figures were taken with agent 0.15 and this is agent 0.23.1: not strictly like for like.
NOT MEASURED
- The radio sticks themselves, USB, the rtl_sdr program that reads them, the agent's main thread
and web page, and the screen dashboard (a browser: about half a Raspberry Pi 4 core by itself).
- Heat. This run lasts minutes; a fanless computer in a hot cabinet may slow down after hours.
- Real radio. Nothing here has been run with a real radio stick on a computer that is not a
Raspberry Pi.
TO SHARE THIS RESULT
Run it again with --out=result.json (the full run, on an idle computer) and send that file:
firmware/bench/results/README.md in the open-ALERT repository says how. The file holds these
figures and a description of the computer — no names, addresses or serial numbers.
